# x0k-ui-control

An agent driving a desktop app sees a picture and guesses where to click. A test
does much the same with a sleep in front of it. Neither can tell what it is looking
at, or whether the picture is from before or after the thing it just did.

`x0k-ui-control` is a small protocol an app answers so that something outside it can
do this properly. An app answers four calls. `offer` says what it can do. `observe`
returns the pixels of one presented frame, the layout tree of that same frame, and
its state. `invoke` runs a named action, and `perform` delivers pointer and key
input aimed at a frame or at a node in its tree. Each answer names the frame that
shows what happened, so a driver never has to sleep and hope.

An app that keeps a history of what it has shown can answer two more. `history`
lists the states it holds, each with the trace ids active when it changed, so a
driver can find the event that caused a state. `navigate` shows one of them, or the
live state again. Going back is for looking: while the app shows the past it
refuses input and any action that is not read-only, and when the driver's session
ends the app shows its live state again. Every observation says whether it shows
the live state or a past one.

A test can also give the app a state to show. `present` takes a whole state, or a
JSON Merge Patch over the live one, with the fingerprint of the state's shape and,
if you like, the head you read it at. A patch over a state that has moved since is
refused. The app is then driven in that state: input works, and a read-only action
runs. Anything else an action would do to the world is simulated, or sent to a
sandbox the app names, and the answer says which. `release` shows the live state
again, and so does the end of the driver's session. The offer says how deeply the
app can be looked into, and what its actions do while a state like this stands.
While a given state stands, the host marks its window with a band at the foot, so
a person at the window can tell it is not the live one.

A screenshot shows where a motion ended; a screencast shows the motion. `cast`
plays a run of timed steps, the same invoke, perform, present and release, at a
frame rate, and keeps every frame for the driver to read with `frames`. An app
that steps its own clock draws frame *n* at exactly its time, however slowly it
renders, so two runs of one cast give the same frames, and a cast can be checked
the way a test checks a value. The Tauri plugin steps the clock of its page: its
animations, transitions, timers and `Date`.

Two hosts answer it today: x0k's own shell, which passes every check in the
conformance suite here, and the Tauri plugin in this repository, which answers for
a Tauri app's web page through the in-page library it carries. One app outside x0k
answers the suite through the plugin. Nobody has written a host of their own yet,
so you would be the first, and the parts of the protocol that only these two have
leaned on are the parts most likely to be wrong.

## What you get

A node in the layout tree has an id that lasts from frame to frame for as long as
that part of the surface stands, so a driver can hold on to "the send button" rather
than a coordinate. Its bounds are in the capture's pixels, and they say what shows,
not where the widget was laid out, so a button scrolled out of view does not get
clicked. A mark drawn on a frame resolves to the nodes it covers, which is how a
person can point at something and have an agent know what they meant.

The wire is canonical CBOR frames on an operation session. It runs on a Unix socket
for a local app and on WebSocket for a page or a remote one. Every call carries a
W3C `traceparent`, so a driver's action and the app's handling of it land in one
trace.

## Check an app

```sh
cargo run --features websocket --bin ui-conformance -- <socket | ws://address> [<action> [<json>]]
cargo run --features websocket --bin ui-conformance -- --listen <address>
```

`ui-conformance` connects to an app and walks the protocol: the offer, one
observation held to one frame, region and scale, a refused call, going back and
returning when the app keeps a history, giving the app a state to show when it
takes one and, on a socket, an oversized frame and a session that ends while it
shows the past or a given state. Naming an action also checks that the action moves the app and that
observing does not. Each check says which section of the protocol it holds the app
to. A page in a browser cannot accept a connection, so `--listen` waits for the app
to dial in and answer.

`vectors/` holds the same claims as data, one case per file, for a driver or an app
in a language this repository does not cover. `shapes.json` spells each interface,
and its fingerprints are how two sides find out they disagree: a session agrees
operation by operation, so a driver that has fallen behind loses only what changed.

## Answer it from Rust

Implement `UiApp` and serve it:

```rust
impl UiApp for MyApp {
    async fn offer(&self) -> Offer { /* what this app can do */ }
    async fn observe(&self, call: ObserveCall) -> Observation { /* one frame, whole */ }
    async fn invoke(&self, action: &Action, args: Value) -> Outcome { /* run it */ }
    async fn held_frames(&self) -> Vec<HeldFrame> { /* frames input may name */ }
    async fn perform(&self, perform: Perform, resolved: Vec<Resolved>) -> Option<String> {
        /* deliver it, and name the frame after */
    }
}
```

An app with a history also implements `shown`, `history` and `navigate`, and names
`ui/history` in its offer. The endpoint makes the refusals while the app shows the
past, and takes it back to the live state when a session that went back ends. An
app that takes a given state implements `state_shape`, `live_state`, `present` and
`release`. The endpoint checks the state against the shape before the app hears it,
and answers each action as the offer's replay policy says while the state stands.

The hard part is `observe`. Your layout tree and your pixels have to come from one
presented frame, and most toolkits read them from different places at different
times. Getting that right in x0k's shell took a change to the event loop, so expect
to touch yours.

`UiClient` is the other side. This release promises the wire, the vectors and the
suite, and no Rust API, so a crate of yours pinned to this one may have to change.

## What it promises

What an app and a driver may rely on is written down in sections 7 to 10 of
[the protocol decision](decisions/architecture/surfaces/ui-control-channel.md),
for history and given states in sections 1 to 5 of
[the interfaces decision](decisions/architecture/surfaces/ui-interfaces.md),
and for screencasts in sections 2 to 6 and 9 of
[the screencast decision](decisions/architecture/surfaces/ui-screencast.md).
The suite and the vectors name those sections. The rest of the interfaces decision,
such as edges for apps that do not speak the protocol, is not built yet.

The client over WebSocket has been exercised from Rust and from Node. It has not
been run in a browser.

Most of the Rust here is ordinary source. The parts listed below are written

**What it ships.** Every chapter, grouped by what it is about rather than which crate its code lands in.

### The protocol

The values an app and a driver exchange, the endpoint that carries them, and the suite that holds an app to them.

- [x0k-ui-protocol: the values of the UI-control endpoint](implementation/ui-control/protocol.md) — x0k-ui-protocol: what an app and a driver say to each other over the UI-control endpoint (an offer, one observation, an action, a sequence of input, the app's history), and the checks the decisions make before an app runs anything, with conformance vectors any language can run.
- [x0k-ui-endpoint: an app's end and a driver's end of the UI-control endpoint](implementation/ui-control/endpoint.md) — x0k-ui-endpoint: the UI-control endpoint over the operation wire. An app implements its calls, the endpoint routes them and refuses a bad one before the app hears it, and a driver calls them through a client.
- [Who allows a takeover: a host's configuration of its endpoint](implementation/ui-control/takeover.md) — x0k-ui-endpoint's takeover configuration: a list of rules and a default answer (ask, allow, refuse) that decides whether a driver's takeover, or a stepped screencast's hold, asks the person, holds without asking or is refused; one value every host builds its endpoint with.
- [The endpoint over a WebSocket](implementation/ui-control/websocket.md) — The UI-control endpoint's frames over a WebSocket, as a byte stream either side can dial, so an app in a browser or a webview answers exactly as one on a unix socket does.
- [The conformance suite, over the endpoint](implementation/ui-control/conformance.md) — The UI-control suite as a program: pointed at an app's socket, it holds the app to ui-control-channel §8 to §10 and ui-interfaces §2 to §5 over the endpoint alone, so any app in any language runs it against itself.

### The operation wire

The frame every call is, the session calls run on, and the carriers it runs over.

- [The operation wire: its frame](implementation/sync/operation-wire.md) — The operation wire's frame: one canonical CBOR map that names its call, kind and operation and carries the side-effect class, the deadline, the trace context and the argument. A frame decodes to exactly the frame that was encoded. On a socket it is a four-byte big-endian length and then its body; a reader refuses a frame over its endpoint's cap before it reads the body, and refuses malformed or unknown content by naming the byte or the field. One listener tells this wire from the older local protocol on the same socket by its first five bytes.
- [The operation wire anywhere: frames and openings with no socket](implementation/sync/operation-wire-anywhere.md) — x0k-operation-wire: the part of the operation session that needs no socket, so a page in a browser drives the same wire a native process does. It spells calls and wakes as frames, cuts bytes into the same frames however a carrier splits them, says what an answer tells its caller, and agrees on shapes at an opening. It reads, writes and waits for nothing, depends on the value model alone, and builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown. It is the home of the side-effect class every frame carries.
- [The operation wire: a session's calls](implementation/sync/operation-session.md) — The session that carries operation frames over one connection, both ways at once. A caller keeps many calls in flight and matches each answer by its own call id. A call past its deadline, or on a connection that has ended, is answered unknown; one past the in-flight bound is refused before the callee hears it. The session opens by agreeing on shapes operation by operation, carries subscriptions whose wakes coalesce and resume from what was read, and lets only a forwarder name whom it asks for.
- [The operation wire over a WebSocket](implementation/sync/websocket-carrier.md) — A WebSocket as the byte stream an operation-wire session runs on, either side dialling, so a page in a browser speaks the same canonical CBOR frames as a process on a unix socket.

### A web page and a Tauri app

The library a page answers with, the design it follows, and the plugin that serves a Tauri app's page as its endpoint.

- [A webview on the UI-control endpoint](implementation/ui-control/webview.md) — How a web page in a Tauri webview or a browser tab answers the UI-control endpoint: the page holds its own frame producers still while its host captures, so the layout, the state and the pixels of one observation come from one page state; input goes through the platform's own input path; and a page reaches its endpoint through its host over IPC, or by dialing out over a WebSocket.
- [The page's layout walk: nodes, ids and bounds](implementation/ui-control/page-walk.md) — The in-page library's layout walk: which DOM elements become layout nodes, with roles and names from dom-accessibility-api, how a node keeps its id while its element stands, and how bounds reach the capture's pixels at the scale the capture shows. A test holds the walk's observations of a probe page and of 0k.computer's web UI to the conformance suite's observation claims, in WebKitGTK and headless Chromium.
- [The page's hold: one page state for one capture](implementation/ui-control/page-hold.md) — The in-page library's hold and epoch: a page names its frame by an epoch that rises whenever its state may have changed, and holds its own frame producers still while its host captures, so the capture and the read come from one page state. A probe page test holds this in headless Chromium over CDP and in WebKitGTK, and is red without the hold.
- [The page's answers: offer, observe and invoke](implementation/ui-control/page-answer.md) — The in-page library's entry: a page installs the library with its app name and its state, declares its named actions, and hands its host what it declared, what it reads and the run of an action, raw. The host makes the protocol's values: the offer, the state part and the checks, with x0k-ui-protocol's page module, natively in a Rust host and through x0k-ui-protocol-wasm in a JavaScript one. A page that gives present and release hooks takes state fixtures: the library keeps the fixture's handle and the live state as it stood, answers what the page shows while a fixture stands, and lets the page's own code ask whether one stands and hear it change, while the fixture checks stay its host's. The page loads no WebAssembly, so a page whose content security policy forbids it answers every call. A test runs the conformance suite itself against the page in WebKitGTK and headless Chromium, through a JSON-lines link, on a page that allows WebAssembly and on one that forbids it.
- [The checks for a host in JavaScript](implementation/ui-control/page-checks.md) — x0k-ui-protocol's page module as a WebAssembly module, x0k-ui-protocol-wasm: a page's offer, its state part and the checks, as one JSON request and one JSON answer through three exported functions, for a host in JavaScript of a web page that answers the UI-control protocol. The page itself never loads it.
- [The Tauri plugin: a Tauri app's page, held and captured](implementation/ui-control/tauri-plugin.md) — A Tauri 2 plugin that is the host of the webview design for a Tauri app on Linux and macOS: it injects the in-page library's hold before the page's scripts, asks the page over Tauri's IPC with a fresh nonce per request and drops any answer without it, and takes the capture natively while the page is held, with webkit_web_view_get_snapshot on Linux and WKWebView's takeSnapshot on macOS. It puts input into the page through the platform's own input path, as GDK events synthesized for the webview's widget on Linux and as NSEvents handed to the WKWebView on macOS, so the page's hit-testing and focus decide the target and its events are trusted. It serves the page as the app's UI-control endpoint with x0k-ui-endpoint, whose checks run before the page hears a call, and forwards a state fixture's present and release to the page's own hooks, answering the first frame painted after each, on a socket named for the app in its profile's runtime directory by the rule every endpoint binds by, so a scratch app never binds in the live runtime. It answers a driver's takeover by the host's configuration, asking the person in the page, holding at once or refusing, and while one stands holds the person's own input back from the page until they press Escape. It answers a stepped screencast: for each frame it advances the library's stepped clock to the frame's time and captures the held page natively, so a Tauri app's screencast of one run is the same on every run and at every frame rate. The library's probe test, an input test and the conformance suite over the endpoint hold it against a minimal Tauri app, under Xvfb on Linux and in a window on the Mac's display.

### Screencasts

The values of a cast, the endpoint that plays one, and the clock a page steps so every frame lands at its own time.

- [A screencast: the values of ui/screencast and the checks before anything plays](implementation/ui-control/screencast.md) — x0k-ui-protocol's ui/screencast: cast a run of timed invoke, perform, present and release steps at a frame rate, read chosen frames of the screencast the endpoint holds, and discard it; the offer's screencast field; the frame each step first shows in; the rows and their trace hash; and the checks that refuse a cast by name before anything plays, held to conformance vectors.
- [The endpoint plays a screencast: the hold, the run, the frames, and the app's hooks](implementation/ui-control/endpoint-screencast.md) — x0k-ui-endpoint answers ui/screencast: it checks a cast before anything plays, asks the host's takeover configuration for a stepped cast's hold, plays the run's timed steps through the endpoint's own calls, draws each frame through the app's stepped or streamed hooks, ends the screencast when it settles, reaches its longest time or a step is refused, and holds one screencast per session for frames and discard.
- [The page's stepped clock: one screencast time for every source of motion](implementation/ui-control/page-clock.md) — The in-page library's stepped clock: a screencast time the host advances by one frame per frame, which every Web Animation, CSS transition, animation-frame callback, timer, performance.now, Date and SVG animation of the page follows, with the page's fetches and IPC counted as work a frame waits for within a bound, so a stepped run draws the same frames on a rerun, at any frame rate and under any load. A probe page test holds this in WebKitGTK and headless Chromium, and is red with one timer the clock does not step.

### Where an endpoint lives

The runtime directory an endpoint binds in, and the rule that keeps a scratch process out of the live one.

- [x0k-runtime-dir: a stack's own runtime directory](implementation/tooling/runtime-dir.md) — x0k-runtime-dir: the leaf that resolves a stack's runtime directory, where its sockets live, from the data root, the profile and the pin the environment carries, and keeps a scratch process out of the live root's runtime. It depends on nothing heavier than dirs, so a crate outside the root workspace, such as the Tauri plugin, binds by the same rule as x0k's own processes.
- [x0k-test-process: whether this process is a test's](implementation/tooling/test-process.md) — x0k-test-process: the leaf that says whether this process is a test's, where a cargo test binary's profile directory is, and where the operator's x0k root is, so a guard in any crate, however lean, can keep a test off the operator's live state.

## Where it comes from

This repository is projected from [x0k](https://0k.computer), a local-first system
that runs the same code. A change proposed here comes back as a proposal against
x0k's sources and appears in this repository on the next projection.

If you have an app an agent should be able to work, and you find you need something
this protocol cannot say, that is what I want to hear about.
